summary: This informational RFC describes a URN namespace for ucode, an identifier system for objects and places, enabling its use in Internet software and devices.

eli5.summary: A name format for giving every object and place its own ID code, so it can be written like a web name.

questions: how to use ucode on the internet
subtitle: A name format for identifying real-world objects with tags.

tldr.problem: ucode is a 128-bit identifier system for tagging objects and places, managed by Japan's Ubiquitous ID Center. Developers wanted to use ucode with Internet protocols but needed an official URN (Uniform Resource Name) namespace to do so.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6588 registers 'ucode' as a formal URN namespace identifier, defining the syntax, structure, uniqueness guarantees and resolution process for ucode identifiers in the format urn:ucode:_<32-hex-digits>.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now embed ucode identifiers in tags (RFID, optical codes, infrared) and reference them on the Internet as URNs, enabling small organizations and individuals to label objects without expensive licensing of existing identifier systems.

facts.label: Managing organization
facts.value: Ubiquitous ID Center, sub-organization of T-Engine Forum

today: RFC 6588 remains the formal registration of the ucode URN namespace. The namespace is actively used by applications and devices that need to identify physical objects and places, particularly in the Internet of Things (IoT) domain, though it remains more common in Asia than in other regions. The resolution process continues to operate through the Ubiquitous ID Center.

sections.title: What is ucode?
sections.content: ucode is a 128-bit identifier system for objects and places, managed by the Ubiquitous ID Center, a sub-organization of Japan's T-Engine Forum. The identifier was created to fill a gap where existing identifier standards did not fit application needs or had allocation policies that were too restrictive for small and medium enterprises (SMEs), academic research labs, or individual users. The basic ucode length is 128 bits (16 bytes, or 32 hexadecimal digits), and it is extensible in 128-bit increments if longer identifiers are needed. ucode can be embedded in many types of tags: RFID tags, 2D optical codes, infrared markers, and even sound sources. Unlike identifiers that encode meaning in their bit structure, ucode is opaque—any relevant information about the object is stored separately on a resolution server reachable over the Internet. Applications using ucode take advantage of Internet connectivity; for example, a smartphone can scan a QR code containing ucode, query a server to retrieve information about the object, and display it to the user. The ucode system was designed to be compatible with ITU-T Recommendation F.771 (multimedia information access triggered by tag-based identification) and ITU-T Recommendation H.621 (architecture for such systems).
sections.eli5: ucode is a number you can put on a physical thing—a tag on a product, a label on a place. Anybody can get numbers, unlike expensive barcodes. Software looks up the number on the internet to find information about the thing.

sections.title: The URN Namespace and Syntax
sections.content: A URN (Uniform Resource Name) is a persistent identifier that can be used on the Internet, similar to a URL but not bound to a physical location. The RFC registers ucode as a formal URN Namespace Identifier (NID), enabling ucode to be used in the format urn:ucode:identifier. The syntax is defined in ABNF (Augmented Backus-Naur Form) as: ucode URNs take the form urn:ucode:_ followed by one or more 32-character hexadecimal strings (for future extensibility beyond the current 128 bits). For example, a 128-bit ucode with the hexadecimal value 0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF is written as urn:ucode:_0123456789ABCDEF0123456789ABCDEF. The underscore prefix is required to make the identifier compatible with XML tag naming rules, which do not allow tags to start with a digit. The entire URN is case-sensitive, and only capital letters A through F are allowed in hexadecimal digits, not lowercase. The namespace conforms to RFC 2141 (URN Syntax) and RFC 3986 (URI Generic Syntax).
sections.eli5: A ucode URN is like a web address for a physical object. It always starts with urn:ucode: followed by the 32-digit code. The underscore at the start lets it work with XML.

sections.title: How ucode is Managed and Resolved
sections.content: The Ubiquitous ID Center maintains the ucode namespace and assigns identifiers in a way that guarantees uniqueness. Uniqueness is assured because all identifiers are assigned from a single registry managed by the Center. Identifiers are never reassigned, and the binding between a ucode and its assigned owner is permanent, regardless of organizational changes or assignment periods. Subspace allocation and delegation are possible: the Ubiquitous ID Center can sub-delegate assignment authority to other organizations. All assignment follows the ucode Management Implementing Procedures (UCDMIP) established by the Center. Identifier resolution—looking up what a ucode refers to—is currently handled by the ucode Resolution Protocol (UCSURP), which is published by the Center. The RFC notes that the resolution process will be enhanced using newer recommendations from ITU-T and standards from ISO in the future. Applications that encounter a ucode URN can use standard URN resolution mechanisms to query a resolver server and obtain metadata about the object or place the ucode identifies.
sections.eli5: The Ubiquitous ID Center keeps the master list of codes and makes sure each one is unique. When a program finds a code, it can ask a server 'what is this code for?' and get back information about the thing.

sections.title: Benefits for Small Organizations and Communities
sections.content: The URN namespace registration enables ucode to be used in Internet protocols and software for the first time. Before this RFC, ucode was managed outside the IETF framework and could not be formally referenced in Internet specifications. With a registered URN namespace, ucode can be stored directly in tags designed to store URNs, metadata about objects can be exchanged using standard formats, and application developers can build ucode support into widespread platforms. The RFC emphasizes that this is particularly beneficial for small-scale providers, SMEs, academic research labs, and individual users who would otherwise have to use existing identifier systems that require expensive licensing or membership fees. Because ucode assignment is open to anyone who applies to the Ubiquitous ID Center or purchases pre-assigned tags from certified providers, the system provides an alternative to closed identifier systems. Applications can now be developed by client software for many types of devices, including smartphones and mobile terminals. The RFC also notes that the resolution servers and applications will be available to general users with appropriate access control, enabling widespread adoption.
sections.eli5: Small groups and individuals can now use ucode like big companies use barcodes. The internet recognizes it as a real identifier system. This is cheaper and more flexible than traditional bar codes.
